content: A review found that infants exposed to TB who showed evidence of infection but did not receive TPT had an 18% chance of developing TB disease within two years of being identified as a contact. Contrary to earlier estimates suggesting lower risk in children aged 2–5 years, this study revealed that this age group also had a high risk of developing TB within two years, at 19%. The effectiveness of TPT in preventing TB disease progression was estimated to be 91% in children and adolescents with TB infection. Another significant finding was that 61% of children and adolescents, and 83% of children under five years old with TB infection, developed TB disease within weeks of the initial contact investigation. Younger children, particularly those under two years of age, were found to be at especially high risk of disease progression following infection. However, contact investigations often reach children too late to prevent disease. Given that 80% of pediatric TB deaths occur in children under five years old, early diagnosis of infectious adults and timely TB screening, diagnosis, and treatment of child contacts are critical strategies to reduce TB-related disease and mortality in children. Studies emphasize the importance of contact investigation. For example, the PHOENIx feasibility study conducted in eight high TB-burden countries demonstrated that contact investigation identified new TB disease in 12% of contacts, with a TB infection prevalence of 72% (defined by positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay). Screening household contacts for TB disease is considered a high-priority, cost-effective strategy. Contact investigation not only links individuals to effective interventions such as TB treatment and TPT but also helps prevent transmission and improves treatment outcomes. It is a key strategy for TB prevention and control, offering significant health and financial benefits to families. TB in a household can have severe social and economic consequences, including catastrophic costs due to income loss or healthcare expenses. Offering TPT to all household members simultaneously, while the index patient is still receiving treatment, can enhance the understanding and impact of TPT and improve cost-effectiveness through interventions like home visits. In settings with high HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of TB patients should be counseled and tested for HIV. In low HIV-prevalence settings, household members and close contacts with symptoms suggestive of TB disease may be offered HIV counseling and testing as part of their clinical evaluation. All household contacts of an index case who is living with HIV should also be counseled and tested for HIV. Contact investigation is essential for identifying undiagnosed TB cases, reducing treatment delays, and preventing onward transmission. It also improves access to TPT for child, adolescent, and adult contacts. National TB programs should include contact investigation as a standard component, as it is a good public health practice and critical for managing infectious diseases like TB and COVID-19. Ministries of health should invest in strengthening health system capacity to conduct contact investigations. If mechanisms for identifying young children and people living with HIV with TB disease and infection are already in place, these can be expanded to include contacts aged five years and older. If such mechanisms are lacking, necessary human and financial resources should be allocated to establish effective contact investigation systems. Budgeting tools have been developed to assist health ministries and organizations in planning and implementing contact investigation activities. These tools focus on costs related to additional health workers, training, community sensitization campaigns, linking child contacts under five years to facilities for TPT initiation, and monitoring and evaluation. However, they do not include costs for linking contacts aged five years and older to TPT initiation facilities or general TB program costs. Key steps in contact investigation include providing standardized guidance, defining roles for healthcare workers, capturing data elements, and using tools to identify contacts and record outcomes. Contact investigation can be implemented at the community or health facility level, depending on the context. For community-based models, approval for home visits should be sought from the index patient. Counseling and education about the benefits of TPT and the risks of not taking it should be central to the process. Confidentiality must be maintained throughout, and national guidelines on data protection, privacy, and informed consent should be followed. Examples of successful contact investigation programs include the CaP-TB project in sub-Saharan Africa and the Vikela Ekhaya program in Eswatini. These initiatives demonstrated the feasibility and effectiveness of community-based TB contact management in improving TB screening and TPT delivery. Challenges such as financial constraints, lack of human resources, and transportation barriers were addressed through dedicated resources, advocacy, and mixed models of facilityand community-based approaches. Lessons learned highlight the importance of dedicated human resources, effective planning, and community engagement in ensuring the success of contact investigation programs.
